drills.q: Decode this JWT header without tooling: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9. What does this prove about JWT security?
drills.a: Restoring padding and base64-decoding gives {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}. This proves header/payload provide zero confidentiality -- anyone can decode them with base64 -d or jwt.io with no secret. Security comes entirely from correct signature verification, not from the encoding.

drills.q: When would you choose HS256 over RS256, and when is that choice a mistake?
drills.a: HS256 is correct when exactly one party issues and verifies tokens. It's a mistake once a second, less-trusted verifier needs the key, since HS256's verification key is also its signing key -- giving it out grants forgery capability, not just verification.

drills.q: Walk through JWKS-based key rotation with zero verifier redeploy required.
drills.a: Issuer generates a new keypair, publishes it alongside the old public key in JWKS, starts signing new tokens with the new kid. Verifiers cache JWKS and refetch on TTL expiry or kid cache-miss, picking up the new key automatically. Old key must stay in JWKS until every token signed with it has passed exp, or removing it early causes an immediate 401 spike.

drills.q: Why does a verifier need leeway, and how much is too much?
drills.a: Clocks between issuing and verifying hosts drift by seconds normally, so a valid token can appear prematurely expired on a slightly-ahead verifier clock. 30-60s absorbs normal drift; beyond a couple minutes you meaningfully widen the window a token you want treated as expired stays accepted.

drills.q: A JWT payload embeds a user's 40 group memberships. What breaks, and why?
drills.a: The token grows into low kilobytes and, sent as a header/cookie on every request, risks colliding with header-size limits (a few KB to ~16KB depending on LB/CDN/webserver), producing 431 Request Header Fields Too Large under normal traffic. It also means every membership change requires re-issuing the token to take effect.

drills.q: What's the actual signature-size difference between RS256 and ES256, and when does it matter enough to switch?
drills.a: RS256 (RSA-2048): ~256 raw bytes (~342 b64 chars). ES256 (P-256): 64 raw bytes (~86 b64 chars), ~4x smaller. Matters in bandwidth/header-size-constrained contexts (mobile, very high QPS); mostly noise for typical web/API traffic. Historically thinner library support and ECDSA implementation bug history are the reasons it isn't the universal default.

drills.q: A token has aud='internal-admin-tool' but is presented to your public customer API, same issuer, same key, signature verifies. Should it be allowed?
drills.a: No. A valid signature only proves who signed it, not who it's for. Without an explicit aud check, a token scoped for one service authenticates against a completely different service sharing the same issuer -- a real, recurring bug class in systems with a shared IdP across multiple services.

drills.q: Why does jti matter even though it's not required for basic JWT validity?
drills.a: Without a unique per-token identifier there's no way to deny-list or flag one SPECIFIC compromised token -- you'd have to block by sub (the whole user's sessions) or skip fine-grained revocation entirely. jti gives that hook, at the cost of reintroducing a per-request deny-list lookup if checked universally.

drills.q: You're adding support for a third-party partner to verify your tokens. What changes about your algorithm choice and key management?
drills.a: If currently on HS256, this forces migration to RS256/ES256 -- you can't safely hand a third party your HMAC secret since that grants forging capability over your whole token space. With asymmetric signing you publish only the public key via JWKS. Also consider a distinct aud value so partner-scoped tokens can't be replayed against internal services.

drills.q: Design token validation for a service that must accept both RS256 (primary IdP) and HS256 (legacy system, being phased out) during a migration window. What's the risk and how do you contain it?
drills.a: The risk is algorithm confusion: a single verification path accepting both algorithms without strict separation lets an attacker try an HMAC forgery hoping the verifier is lenient about which key applies to which algorithm. Safe design: two fully separate verification paths keyed by a pre-checked discriminator like iss, never one decode() call with algorithms=['RS256','HS256'] and ambiguous key selection. Set a hard deadline to retire the HS256 path.

drills.q: Is it safe to use the unverified iss claim to select which key/algorithm path to verify against?
drills.a: Only if each path's key is scoped so a forged iss value can't trick the verifier into using a more permissive key -- you still fully verify the signature end-to-end afterward on whichever path was selected. iss must never be treated as authorization by itself before the signature check completes.
